subject: technology
essential_question: How can understanding data, media, and source responsibility help us explain, decide, create, or solve something that matters?
standards: Michigan Computer Science: Data and Analysis
project_brief: Create a transparent data story with cited or original media and an AI/source verification note. This is the grade 5 culminating project for "Data, Media, and Source Responsibility" (ma-g5-technology-u05, unit 5), built around collecting simple data, tables and charts, image and media rights, search strategies, and source credibility. Collect or use a small, fictional or already-approved data set related to collecting simple data, tables and charts, image and media rights, and search strategies, and turn it into a labeled visual with a one-paragraph, evidence-based conclusion.
requirements: Address every topic listed for this unit: collecting simple data, tables and charts, image and media rights, search strategies, source credibility, and AI-generated content checks.
Meet the performance task as written: Create a transparent data story with cited or original media and an AI/source verification note.
Show your work or process, not just a final result — a process note, sketch log, commit history, or draft trail.
Complete the checklist in this package before submitting.
primary_task: Collect or use a small, fictional or already-approved data set related to collecting simple data, tables and charts, image and media rights, and search strategies, and turn it into a labeled visual with a one-paragraph, evidence-based conclusion.
test_or_check_criteria: Every claim or design choice in the submission can be traced to collecting simple data or another named topic from this unit — nothing is left unexplained.
The submission runs, displays, or demonstrates correctly on at least two different sample inputs or scenarios the student chooses.
No real password, API key, account credential, precise location, or other real personal/system data appears anywhere in the submission — fictional or sandbox examples only.
The student can explain, in their own words, why each step or decision was made, not just that it works.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: This project never touches a real account, a real password or API key, a live production system, or another person's real data. Use fictional names, sandbox environments, local files, or already-approved sample data throughout. Submit code, screenshots of your own sandbox, diagrams, or a written walkthrough — a live public deployment is never required.

copyright_and_authorship: The final submitted work must remain your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI assistant may help you plan, explain a concept, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but may not produce the graded work itself. Never request, store, or submit a real password, API key, access token, or other real credential; use only fictional accounts and sandboxed or offline systems.
remediation: If the project stalls, step back to the smallest version of the task: rebuild just the part covering collecting simple data in isolation, using a worked example from this unit as a model, then re-attach it to the full project once that smaller piece works and you can explain why.
extension: Once the core project is working, extend it to handle a new constraint or edge case related to tables and charts, or compare two different approaches to the same problem and explain the real tradeoff between them in your own words.
